# Estimating an unknown mean $\mu$, assuming $\sigma$ is known

Suppose we have a population of values for some
quantitative variable $X$, and we know $\sigma
= \sigma_X$ but not $\mu$.  We may

 * know that our population is normal.
 * be able to take an iid sample of size $n\ge 30$.
 
In either case, the Central Limit Theorem and the
general experience of statisticians tells us we
will have a sampling distribution for $\bar X$
that is approximately normal:
$$ \bar X \sim \mbox{Norm}\left(\mu,
  \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right)
  \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
  Z = \frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \sim
  \mbox{Norm}(0,1). $$

Note: There are two standard deviations involved,
here.  There is $\sigma$, the population standard
deviation, and $\sigma/\sqrt n$, the standard
deviation of the sampling distribution of $\bar X$.
Convention is that we give that of the sampling
distribution another name, calling it the
**standard error**.  In this case, we are dealing
with the sampling distribution of $\bar X$, so
we call this second standard deviation the
**standard error of the mean**, or
$$ \mbox{SE}_{\bar X} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}. $$

The command
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
xqnorm(c(0.025,0.975))
```
displays that 95% of values in the standard
normal distribution lie between $Z=-1.96$ and
$Z=1.96$.  The Empirical Rule for normal
distributions says, among other things,
"approximately 95% of values lie within 2 standard
deviations of the mean."  Now we see the more
accurate statement is that "95% of values lie
within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean."

The natural implication is that 95% of values
of $\bar X$ satisfy
$$ -1.96 < \frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
  < 1.96 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
  \bar X - (1.96)\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
  < \mu <  \bar X + (1.96)\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.$$

We call the interval
$$  (\bar X - (1.96)\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},
   \bar X + (1.96)\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}) $$
a 95% confidence interval for $\mu$.

### How to interpret this confidence

We are doing inference in constructing this
interval.  It involves drawing an iid sample,
computing both the mean $\bar X$ and a
**margin of error**
$$ 1.96 \mbox{SE}_{\bar X}
 = 1.96 \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}. $$
This margin of error is added and subtracted
from a value, $\bar X$, that is sample-specific,
in order to obtain lower and upper bounds on the
interval.  Thus, the generation of lower/upper
bounds is the result of a random process.  While
$\mu$ is unknown, it is a fixed quantity which
may or may not be contained between lower and
upper bounds randomly generated.

In this context, what we are 95% confident about
is the method of construction.  We will gather
just one sample (where randomness plays a role),
and follow a deterministic method to obtain
lower/upper bounds to an interval, and $\mu$
may or may not be inside that interval.  We
will not know for certain.  We simply know this
construction method is going to successfully
"capture" $\mu$ in 95% of instances.

### Other levels of confidence.

One can use `qnorm()` to capture different
"interior areas".  The nearest 80% of values
(nearest to the mean) are represented as those
between the 10th and 90th percentiles---those
with Z-scores displayed here:
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
xqnorm(c(0.1,0.9))
```

If we use $z^\ast=1.2816$ in place of
$z^\ast=1.96$ in the calculation of the margin
of error
$$ 1.2816 \mbox{SE}_{\bar X} = 1.2816
 \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}, $$
this change of method of construction changes
the success rate to 80%.  We can choose $z^\ast$
to an desired level of success.

# Hypothesis testing, $\sigma$ known

In hypothesis testing, we ground things with
the null hypothesis
$$ {\mathbf H_0}\colon \mu = \mu_0. $$
That is, we say something like, "$\mu$ is this
value $\mu_0$.  Prove me wrong!"  We may,
actually, walk into the problem with prior
experience that suggests $\mu > \mu_0$, and we
wish to show this alternative is true:
$$ {\mathbf H_a}\colon \mu > \mu_0. $$
We set the level of significance $\alpha$, which
dictates the probability
$$ \alpha = \mbox{P}(\mbox{rejection of}
  \;{\mathbf H_0}
  \,\mid\, {\mathbf H_0}\;\mbox{is true}), $$
and obtain evidence in the form of an iid
random sample.  The particular random sample
generates an instance of a sample mean $\bar X
= \bar x$.  The $p$-value, as before, is 
$$ \mbox{P}(\bar X > \bar x \,\mid\,
  {\mathbf H_0}\;\mbox{is true}) \;=\;
  \mbox{P}\left(Z > \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}
  {\sigma / \sqrt{n}}\right). $$
  
For 2-sided alternative hypotheses, this
expression becomes$p$-value
$$  \mbox{P}\left(|Z|>\left|\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}
  {\sigma / \sqrt{n}}\right|\right) \;=\;
  2 \times \mbox{P}\left(Z>\left|\frac{\bar x-
  \mu_0} {\sigma / \sqrt{n}}\right|\right). $$
If $\alpha = 0.05$, the **rejection region**
corresponds to $\bar X$-values
$$ z = \frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n} < -1.96
  \qquad\mbox{or}\qquad z =
  \frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n} > 1.96. $$
